title: Add valid permissions presets to mock-policy-server
body:
## Summary

Adds five new `managedSettings` presets to the mock policy server that exercise the Copilot SDK's `permissions` managed-settings field, so devs can exercise realistic enterprise permission policies locally without hand-writing JSON.

## Presets added

- **Allow auto-approval only** — `disableBypassPermissionsMode: 'allow-auto-only'` (blocks full allow-all bypass but still permits advisory auto-approval).
- **Deny dangerous shell/file operations** — `deny` list with `Shell(rm -rf *)`, `Shell(curl *)`, `Write(/etc/**)`, `Domain(evil.example.com)`.
- **Ask before publishing or deploying** — `ask` list with `Shell(npm publish *)`, `Shell(git push *)`, `Write(~/**)`.
- **Lockdown: allow only an approved set** — `allow` list intersection combined with `deny`, plus `disableBypassPermissionsMode: 'disable'`.
- Clarified the description of the existing "Disable bypass permissions" preset.

## Validation

Every rule string and preset body was checked against ground truth in `microsoft/copilot-agent-runtime`:

- Validated all preset bodies with Python `jsonschema` against `schema/managed-settings-schema.json` (the same schema the mock server's `--schema` / `schema: true` option enforces).
- Verified each rule string (`Shell(...)`, `Write(...)`, `Read(...)`, `Domain(...)`) against the rule-construction logic in `agentHostManagedRules.ts` and the runtime's `parse_managed_rule` (`src/runtime/src/permissions/managed.rs`), so nothing here would be silently rejected by the runtime's strict grammar.
- Ran the mock server locally on a temporary port with `schema: true` enabled and applied each new preset via `/api/state`; all returned successfully with no schema errors.

title: agent host: anchor side chat forks at the last completed turn
body:
A side chat can branch from a turn that is still running. The host asked the provider to
fork at that active turn, but an active turn is not yet in any provider history. Each
provider then used a different fallback: Copilot inherited all turns, Claude created a
fresh chat, and Codex made an error. Side chats were thus not available for Codex.

The host now anchors the fork at the last completed non-local turn, and the side chat
contribution adds only the turns that the fork cannot carry. Thus the side chat shows the
source conversation one time.

- Adds `resolveLastNonLocalTurnId` to the shared conversation context module. The host and
  the side chat contribution use the same helper, because the two values must agree.
- Anchors an active-turn side chat fork at the last completed non-local turn. The origin
  keeps the identifier of the turn that the user branched from.
- Removes the fork when no completed non-local turn is available, which makes a fresh chat.
  Turn execution uses per-chat queues, thus creation does not wait for the source turn.
- Limits the added context for an active turn to the trailing local turns, the active turn
  message, and the partial response.
- Enables side chats for Codex. No other Codex change is necessary.
- Divides the advertised side chat capability from the end-to-end replay coverage with
  `supportsSideChatsE2E`, which obeys the `supportsChatForkE2E` pattern. The Codex scenario
  stays disabled until focused captures are available.

title: Back off GitHub requests instead of hammering a failing service
body:
## The bug

`GitHubCredentialService` kept no memory of failure. Any failed identity resolution cleared the current generation, so the very next `getCredential()` immediately reissued `GET /user`.

A 401 amplified that. `handleRequestError` invalidates the generation, and both `PullRequestResourceService` and `GitHubQueryService` answer the resulting `onDidInvalidate` by rescheduling **every** fragment and entity at `now` — each of which asks for a credential again. So when `/user` succeeded but real requests kept being refused (an auth outage, or a token GraphQL rejects), this was an unbounded zero-delay loop: roughly one identity request plus nine fragment requests per network round trip, per subscribed pull request, per user, for the whole outage.

The main consumer is `AgentMergeController`, which holds a background pull request subscription per session.

## The fix

New `githubBackoff.ts` holds the concern in one place:

- `GitHubBackoffPolicy` — `{ immediateRetries, base, maximum, jitter, decay? }`
- `gitHubBackoffDelay(policy, scheduler, attempts, minimum?)` — the shared escalating, jittered delay
- `GitHubBackoffGate` — holds back attempts against a subject that keeps failing

Callers **wait** rather than being rejected, so recovery stays automatic once GitHub returns and everyone queued behind one delay shares the single attempt that follows it. Waiters are woken when the record changes instead of sleeping out a stale window, and a caller whose token was replaced mid-wait abandons rather than aborting the replacement''s in-flight request.

A successful `/user` deliberately does **not** clear the record — it only proves identity resolution recovered, and clearing it would reset the delay to zero every round in exactly the loop above. Recovery is signalled by a new token, a new host, or the record decaying (5 min) while nothing fails.

## Also

- **Unified three other escalating retries** onto the same helper: the query service (which previously retried failures at its *normal* poll cadence forever), the capability probe, and `PullRequestResourceService`, which already had an identical inline copy of the formula.
- **Capability probe negative cache** — an unusable probe result was re-probed on *every* capability lookup, and because the fragments that ask still succeed on REST fallbacks nothing throttled it. A degraded result is now reused for an escalating window.
- **Rate limit hints** — a refusal carrying no usable hint recorded no block at all. Now: honour `Retry-After`; otherwise honour `x-ratelimit-reset` only when `x-ratelimit-remaining` is `0` (a secondary limit reports the *primary* hourly window, which would park the account for an hour over a 60s refusal); otherwise apply a 60s floor. Elapsed hints no longer retry immediately.

## Validation

`npm run typecheck-client` clean. 116 tests pass — all of `src/vs/platform/github/test/node` plus the agent merge suites — including new coverage for the escalation under a still-resolving identity call, immediate recovery on re-auth, the query-service escalation, jitter retention when the poll cadence dominates, and the three rate-limit hint shapes.

title: fix(find): set aria-hidden synchronously on reveal to prevent focus exception (closes #235108)
body:
## Summary

- Fixes an accessibility/DOM exception where opening the Find widget triggers:
  `"Blocked aria-hidden on a <textarea> element because the element that just received focus must not be hidden from assistive technology users."`
- Previously, `_reveal()` scheduled setting `aria-hidden` to `false` inside a `setTimeout(..., 0)`, while focusing the child find `<textarea>` input was performed synchronously right after `_start()`. - Now sets `aria-hidden` to `'false'` synchronously in `_reveal()` before any child input element is focused.

Closes #235108

## Validation

- Ran ESLint on `src/vs/editor/contrib/find/browser/findWidget.ts`: passed with 0 errors.

title: managed settings: fix claude enablement
body:
## Summary

Hide the Agent Host Claude provider when `chat.agentHost.claudeAgent.enabled` is disabled by enterprise policy or configuration.

## Problem

When any Copilot managed setting is present, `Claude3PIntegration` resolves `chat.agentHost.claudeAgent.enabled` to `false`. Policy Diagnostics showed the setting was enforced correctly, but the chat session target picker still displayed **Claude**.

The visible entry was not the extension-hosted `claude-code` harness:

- the current Copilot extension no longer contributes that harness; and
- the distro policy metadata already references `github.copilot.chat.claudeAgent.enabled` from the `Claude3PIntegration` owner policy.

The remaining entry came from Agent Host. `shouldSurfaceLocalAgentHostProvider` always returned `true` for Claude, so UI registration ignored the effective enablement setting even though the Agent Host process itself skipped the disabled provider.

## Change

- Gate Agent Host Claude advertisement on `chat.agentHost.claudeAgent.enabled`.
- Treat changes to that setting as provider-preference changes so workbench and Agents window registrations are re-evaluated.
- Extend the focused provider-visibility tests to cover enabled and disabled Claude behavior in both windows.

## Validation

- `npm run transpile-client`
- Targeted ESLint for the changed files
- Agent Host unit suite: 39 passing
- End-to-end Code OSS launch using the Linux `managed-settings.json` channel:
  - Policy Diagnostics reported `Claude3PIntegration` from `Managed Settings: File`

title: fix(find): do not steal focus when syncing globalFindClipboard on pane switch (closes #228767)
body:
## Summary

- Prevents `FindWidget` from erroneously stealing keyboard focus from the text editor when switching panes while `editor.find.globalFindClipboard` is enabled.

Closes #228767

title: Clip the notebook editor to the rounded editor card
body:
With `workbench.experimental.modernUI` enabled the editor part is drawn as a rounded card. A notebook paints square corners on top of it, while a text editor in the same place looks correct.

Notebook editors are not children of the editor part. The widget is parented to a host on the workbench that `OverlayLayoutElement` anchors over the part and clips with `clip-path: content-box`. That host carries no radius, so the clip is a sharp rectangle and `notebook.editorBackground` covers the card corners. Text editors sit inside the part and are clipped by it, which is why only notebooks show this.

Rounding the host makes its content box a rounded rect, so the existing clip follows the card. The widget tags the host with a marker class and keeps the outer edge classes in sync from the part, the same way `OverlayWebview` drives its rules in `floatingPanels.css`, so compact mode is covered as well.

Because the host spans the whole part rather than a single group, this stays correct when the editor is split. A group only loses a corner where it actually meets a corner of the card, and a group in the middle keeps all four square.

title: Round notebook cell surfaces to match the cell outline
body:
Notebook cells draw a rounded outline on `.cell-editor-part::before`, but the surfaces inside it paint square corners, so those corners show past the outline.

Three surfaces are involved. The editor root fills `editor.background` and is `overflow: visible`. Its `.overflow-guard` already clips but carries no radius. The status bar closes the bottom. Because `notebook.cellEditorBackground` differs from `notebook.editorBackground` by design, the square corners are visible on the stock themes too, `#181818` against `#1F1F1F` in Dark Modern.

Matching the radius on each surface is enough on its own, since a background is always clipped to its own border radius.

The rules use child combinators so they only reach the cell's own editor. A descendant selector would also match an editor nested inside the cell, such as a Peek Definition preview, and would give that one the cell radius.

Putting the radius on `.cell-editor-part` together with `overflow: hidden` is not an option instead. The execution progress bar is a child of the part positioned at `top: -3px`, above it, and would be clipped away.

No experimental setting is needed to reproduce this. The rounded cell outline is not behind a flag.

title: Increase hit target of hover zoom buttons
body:
Fixes #233555

## Problem

The increase/decrease hover verbosity buttons (the small `+`/`-` icons that appear in the editor hover when a hover part supports more/less detail) have a very small clickable area. In `hover.css`, the 5px horizontal padding that gives the buttons some breathing room is applied to the `.verbosity-actions-inner` container, not to the buttons themselves, so that padding is dead space — the actual clickable element (the codicon) is only as wide as its ~11px glyph.

## Fix

Move the horizontal padding from `.verbosity-actions-inner` onto the `.codicon` buttons in `src/vs/editor/contrib/hover/browser/hover.css`. Since the container uses `display: flex; flex-direction: column` (default `align-items: stretch`), each button already stretches to the container's content width either way, so the glyph ends up in exactly the same visual position — only now the padding is part of the button's own box and is clickable. This roughly doubles the horizontal hit target (from ~12px to ~22px) with no visual change.

I intentionally left the vertical dimension alone. The two icons form a 22px-tall stack whose height is hardcoded as `iconsHeight` in `handleScroll` (`markdownHoverParticipant.ts`), used to keep the buttons pinned to the bottom of the hover row while scrolling, and the column is clipped with `overflow-y: clip`. Growing the buttons vertically would require updating that constant and would clip on short hover rows, so it's out of scope for this minimal fix.

## Testing

This is a CSS-only change verified by reading the code and reasoning through the box model, not by running a build (no `node_modules` in this checkout, so I couldn't run stylelint or launch VS Code to confirm visually). There's no existing automated test for hit-target sizing in this codebase, so I'm not adding one.

title: Rename from the session header uses the inline title input
Fix false-positive CompletionItem.command deprecation report
body:
Fixes #237861

## Problem

The built-in typescript-language-features extension sets `CompletionItem.command` once, up front, in `provideCompletionItems` (`extensions/typescript-language-features/src/languageFeatures/completions.ts`) and never touches it again in `resolveCompletionItem`. Despite that, resolving a completion item reliably reports `CompletionItem.command` as deprecated ("extension MAY NOT change 'command' of a CompletionItem during resolve"), which is what #237861 asks to fix.

The command is never actually changed. The false positive comes from `CompletionsAdapter.resolveCompletionItem` in `extHostLanguageFeatures.ts`, which converts the item to a wire DTO before and after calling the provider's `resolveCompletionItem`, then diffs `commandIdent`/`commandId`/`commandArguments` on the two DTOs. `CommandsConverter#toInternal` mints a brand new `$ident` on every single conversion for any command with non-empty `arguments` (no memoization keyed on the command object), so `commandIdent` differs across the two conversions even when the underlying `vscode.Command` never changed. Any provider that sets `command` with arguments and also implements `resolveCompletionItem` gets flagged unconditionally.

This dto-based diff was introduced in #186179 ("improve deprecated API reporting"), which replaced an earlier, correct check that compared the raw `vscode.Command` objects directly.

Note that `typescript-language-features` sets `command.arguments` to `[item]` specifically to work around VS Code sometimes applying a completion before `resolveCompletionItem` finishes (#109439) — auto-imports would otherwise be silently dropped on fast accepts. So the fix isn't in the extension; it can't stop passing arguments without regressing that fix.

## Fix

Compare the actual `vscode.Command` objects (captured before and after invoking the provider) instead of the converted DTOs. This is close to the pre-#186179 behavior, with one improvement: the "before" command is snapshotted prior to calling the provider, so an in-place mutation of the same item's `command` is still caught (comparing dto/command only after resolve would miss that case, since resolved and original would be the same object by the time it's read).

## Testing

Added a unit test in `src/vs/workbench/api/test/browser/extHostLanguageFeatures.test.ts` that registers a completion provider whose `command` mirrors the ts/js extension's shape (set once at provide time, argument is the item itself, left untouched in `resolveCompletionItem`), resolves the item, and asserts no `CompletionItem.command` deprecation is reported. The test follows the existing `CodeLens, do not resolve a resolved lens` pattern in the same file, and fails against the pre-fix code (traced manually: the old ident-diff always disagrees across the two conversions).

I was not able to run this test or typecheck the change in my environment — there's no `node_modules` installed and a full install was out of scope for this change. I've traced the RPC call path (`ExtHostLanguageFeatures.$resolveCompletionItem` → `MainThreadLanguageFeatures`'s registered provider → `CompletionItem.resolve` in `editor/contrib/suggest`) by hand to confirm the test exercises the real code path, but this hasn't been machine-verified.

title: Scroll hover widget when dragging selection past its edge
body:
Fixes #239704

## Problem

Starting a text selection with the mouse inside the hover widget and dragging past its top/bottom edge does nothing useful: the content doesn't scroll and the hover disappears.

The disappearing part turned out to be the more interesting bug. `ContentHoverController._onEditorMouseMove` hides the hover while dragging (`this._isMouseDown && !this._shouldKeepHoverWidgetVisible(...)`), and the comment right above it says this is meant for drags that *started outside* the hover widget so the widget doesn't cover a selection made in the editor text. But the check never actually looked at where the mousedown happened — only where the mouse currently is — so a selection that starts inside the hover and drags past its edge hits the same "hide" path.

Separately, even with the hover staying open, there was no way to scroll it: `HoverWidget`'s scrollable content uses `overflow: hidden` (Monaco's usual custom-scrollbar approach), which also disables the browser's native drag-to-autoscroll for text selection.

## Fix

- `contentHoverController.ts`: track whether the mousedown that's currently held started on the content hover widget (`_isMouseDownOnContentHoverWidget`). If it did, dragging outside the widget's bounds keeps it open instead of hiding/recomputing it.
- `hoverWidget.ts` (`src/vs/base/browser/ui/hover/hoverWidget.ts`): while a selection drag is active, auto-scroll the content when the mouse crosses near the top/bottom edge, with scroll speed proportional to how far past the edge the mouse is. This follows the same shape as `listView.ts`'s existing DND autoscroll (`animateDragAndDropScrollTop`), using `dom.animate` to drive the loop each frame and clamping handled by `ScrollState`, the same as the existing `scrollUp`/`scrollDown` methods on `ContentHoverWidget`.

This lives on the shared `HoverWidget` base class (which owns `contentsDomNode`/`scrollbar`), so it applies to both the editor content/glyph hovers and the generic workbench hover built on top of it, not just the editor content hover.

Known limitation: the scroll is driven by `mousemove`, so if you drag past the edge and then hold the mouse still, the content keeps scrolling but the selection itself won't keep extending until the mouse moves again (same as it currently behaves once the drag re-enters the hover). Making the selection extend on a stationary mouse would need synthetic mousemove dispatch or `caretRangeFromPoint`/`selection.extend()`, which felt out of scope for this fix.

## Testing

Typechecked both changed files directly (`tsc --noEmit`) — the only diagnostics were pre-existing `*.css` side-effect-import errors that show up for any file in this checkout since there's no `node_modules`/build step here, unrelated to this change.

There's no existing test under `src/vs/editor/contrib/hover/test` that exercises mouse drag/selection, and jsdom doesn't produce real layout (`scrollHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`), so there wasn't a meaningful unit test to add for the scroll math itself. I was not able to manually verify the drag interaction in a running build in this environment — the fix is based on reading the mouse-hide logic and the existing drag-to-scroll pattern in `listView.ts`.

title: Load ESM extensions synchronously so codeLoadingTime is accurate
body:
Fixes #332556

### The problem

`codeLoadingTime` for an ESM extension could include time spent loading *other* extensions.

The module itself isn't slow — its evaluation is already serialised by Node. What's slow is the `await`. When several extensions activate together they all start their timer at once, and the one that finishes first still can't resume until whoever is evaluating gives the thread back. Measured on a trivial module loading next to a 300ms one:

```
actual evaluation timeline (from inside the modules):
    eval:probe        0ms      <- evaluated instantly
    eval:burn:start   0ms
    eval:burn:end   300ms

what the timer saw:
    probe   started 0ms  settled 300ms  -> reported 300ms
```

The number isn't only used for telemetry — it also drives the "slow extension" warnings in the Running Extensions editor and the extension hover, so ESM extensions could be blamed for their neighbours' startup cost.

### The fix

Load ESM extensions with Node's synchronous `require(esm)` path, the same one Node uses when CJS code requires an ESM module. Nothing else can run during a synchronous load, so the timer covers that extension's own work by construction.

ESM modules using top-level `await` can't be loaded synchronously. Node reports those with `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE` *before evaluating anything*, so those fall back to `import()` with nothing half-loaded behind them. `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` falls back the same way, so a runtime without `require(esm)` keeps working.

This also moves the localization setup out of the timed section. It was sitting inside the measurement and inflating the number for CJS extensions too.

### Numbers

40 ESM extensions activating together, a third of them doing ~40ms of real work:

| | total | reported median | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| `import()` (today) | 651ms | 609ms | 650ms |
| `require(esm)` | 632ms | 2ms | 43ms |

Accurate, and not slower.

### What extensions using top-level await get

Both attempts are timed as one span, because the failed `require` is what parses the module graph — usually most of the cost — and `import()` then reuses it from cache. That parsing is measured exactly, since it's synchronous. Only whatever runs after the `await` resumes is wall clock and can still pick up other extensions' work.

So these extensions get a partly accurate number rather than no benefit. Timing both attempts matters: timing only the `import()` reports roughly zero for them, which would quietly hide a genuinely expensive extension.

### Notes for whoever reads the telemetry

- `codeLoadingTime` keeps its name but now means "what this extension cost" rather than "how long until it was ready". Values will step down, correctly, so dashboards trending it across the release will show a discontinuity.
- The "how long until it was ready" view isn't lost: the `willLoadExtensionCode` / `didLoadExtensionCode` perf marks still cover the whole wait and already ship via `startup.timer.mark`. No new telemetry fields.
- `activateCallTime` brackets a synchronous call and was never affected by any of this. `activateResolvedTime` waits on the extension's own promise and still includes whatever else runs during that wait — untouched here. Both "slow extension" UI surfaces sum `codeLoadingTime + activateCallTime` and leave `activateResolvedTime` out, so they're now correct.

### One behaviour change worth knowing about

For a module with a `default` export, `require(esm)` adds an `__esModule: true` marker to the namespace that `import()` doesn't:

| module | `require(esm)` | `import()` |
|---|---|---|
| only named exports | `[activate, deactivate]` | `[activate, deactivate]` |
| has a default export | `[__esModule, activate, default]` | `[activate, default]` |

`activate` and `deactivate` are identical either way, so activation itself is unaffected. It's only visible when an extension has no `activate` function, because then the module namespace is handed out as that extension's `exports` — a consumer doing `__esModule ? mod.default : mod` interop would start unwrapping `.default`. Narrow, but it is a public API surface change.

### Verified

`require(esm)` keeps working with the ext host's `registerHooks` interception for the `vscode` bare specifier (including the `data:` URL API instances), returns the same module namespace object as `import()` with live bindings intact, and preserves `import.meta.url` / `resolve` / `dirname` and module-evaluation error shapes. Builtin imports, JSON import attributes, `createRequire`, ESM↔CJS interop, circular imports and `"type": "module"` entry points all load synchronously; only top-level `await` falls back.

Worth exercising in CI on all three platforms for extensions loaded out of an `.asar`.

<!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: https://opensource.microsoft.com/codeofconduct/ -->
<!-- 🕮 Read our guide about submitting issues: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/Submitting-Bugs-and-Suggestions -->
<!-- 🔎 Search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. -->
<!-- 🧪 Test using the latest Insiders build to see if your issue has already been fixed: https://code.visualstudio.com/insiders/ -->
<!-- 💡 Instead of creating your report here, use 'Report Issue' from the 'Help' menu in VS Code to pre-fill useful information. -->
<!-- 🔧 Launch with `code --disable-extensions` to check. -->
Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes

- VS Code Version: 1.135.0-insider (0052619e71feb774a574b37f4f2ea20c36547373) and 1.129.0-insider (174edf23f6d4eaf609df4a4619a1c8b523939cfd)
- OS Version: macOS 26.5.2 (25F84), arm64

`blob_storage` in my Code - Insiders profile had grown to 13 GB. Tracing it back, `getWorkerBootstrapUrl` creates a blob URL for every web worker and nothing ever revokes it.

A registered blob URL holds a strong reference to its `Blob` until it is revoked or the document unloads. So every worker creation permanently retains its bootstrap script, which is currently around 1.1 MB because the bootstrap inlines the whole NLS message table and `product.json`.

`application.experimental.rendererProfiling` was enabled on my install by the startup experiment (my `settings.json` did not contain the setting), and `rendererAutoProfiler` builds up to three `CpuProfileAnalysisWorker`s per triggered session. Over a few days that came to roughly 12,800 retained blobs.

## Steps to Reproduce

You do not need a slow machine for this, since the long task can be forced.

1. Launch an isolated instance with no extensions:

   ```
   "/Applications/Visual Studio Code - Insiders.app/Contents/MacOS/Code - Insiders" \
     --user-data-dir=/tmp/vsc-repro --extensions-dir=/tmp/vsc-repro-ext \
     --remote-debugging-port=9333 --new-window
   ```

   (Keep that path short. The Electron IPC socket path is capped at 103 characters and a longer one fails with `EINVAL`.)

2. Set `"application.experimental.rendererProfiling": true` in that instance.

3. Open Help > Toggle Developer Tools and install a probe on the console:

   ```js
   const created = [], revoked = [];
   const c = URL.createObjectURL.bind(URL), r = URL.revokeObjectURL.bind(URL);
   URL.createObjectURL = function (o) { const u = c(o); created.push({ url: u, size: o.size }); return u; };
   URL.revokeObjectURL = function (u) { revoked.push(u); return r(u); };
   globalThis.__probe = { created, revoked };
   ```

4. Force a long task past the `perfBaseline * 10` threshold:

   ```js
   setTimeout(() => { const t0 = performance.now(); while (performance.now() - t0 < 3000) {} }, 0);
   ```

5. Wait about 20 seconds, then read the probe:

   ```js
   [globalThis.__probe.created.length, globalThis.__probe.revoked.length]
   ```

**Expected:** the blob URL created for a worker is revoked once that worker has loaded.

**Actual:** 3 blob URLs created per profiling session, 0 revoked. Repeat step 4 and it adds 3 more every time, with no bound.

## What I measured

Two long tasks per arm, isolated profile, no extensions:

| Version | `rendererProfiling` | blobs created | revoked | size each |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.129.0-insider | `true` | 6 | **0** | 1,109,433 B |
| 1.129.0-insider | `false` | 0 | 0 | |
| 1.135.0-insider | `true` | 6 | **0** | 1,197,782 B |
| 1.135.0-insider | `false` | 0 | 0 | |

Reading the blob contents back confirms they are worker bootstraps. Each one begins `/*CpuProfileAnalysisWorker*/globalThis._VSCODE_NLS_MESSAGES = [...`.

Console output for the `true` arms:

```
[perf] Render performance baseline is 12ms
[perf] Renderer reported VERY LONG TASK (3000ms), starting profiling session '5a9e25d1-...'
[perf] Renderer reported VERY LONG TASK (3000ms), starting profiling session 'da7a0a87-...'
```

Three blobs per session lines up with the retry loop in `rendererAutoProfiler`, which calls `analyseBottomUp` up to three times and builds a fresh worker each time.

## Cause

In `src/vs/platform/webWorker/browser/webWorkerServiceImpl.ts`, at `08a1ad01b35e41b7412e2290c010cda68bdf6333`.

`getWorkerBootstrapUrl` returns a fresh blob URL (line 117):

```ts
	]).join('')], { type: 'application/javascript' });
	return URL.createObjectURL(blob);
```

`_createWorker` puts it in a local that goes out of scope right away (lines 36-38):

```ts
	const workerUrlWithNls = getWorkerBootstrapUrl(descriptor.label, workerRunnerUrl, this._getWorkerLoadingFailedErrorMessage(descriptor));
	const worker = new Worker(ttPolicy ? ttPolicy.createScriptURL(workerUrlWithNls) as unknown as string : workerUrlWithNls, { name: descriptor.label, type: 'module' });
	return whenESMWorkerReady(worker);
```

The URL is never stored anywhere, so `WebWorker`'s dispose (line 164) has nothing to revoke:

```ts
	this._register(toDisposable(() => {
		this.worker?.then(w => {
			w.onmessage = null;
			w.onmessageerror = null;
			w.removeEventListener('error', errorHandler);
			w.terminate();
		});
		this.worker = null;
	}));
```

`revokeObjectURL` does not appear anywhere in that file.

The correct pattern with the same API is already in the repo. `perfBaseline` in `src/vs/workbench/services/timer/browser/timerService.ts` (line 593):

```ts
	const blobUrl = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
	const worker = createBlobWorker(blobUrl, { name: 'perfBaseline' });
	return new Promise<number>(resolve => {
		worker.onmessage = e => resolve(e.data.value);
	}).finally(() => {
		worker.terminate();
		URL.revokeObjectURL(blobUrl);
	});
```

#253663 fixed the related problem of these workers not being terminated, but it did not touch the blob URL.

## Suggestion

`whenESMWorkerReady` already resolves after the bootstrap has finished importing the real worker script, and that is the point where the blob URL stops being needed. It rejects through `worker.onerror`, so `.finally` covers the load-failure path too:

```ts
	const worker = new Worker(ttPolicy ? ttPolicy.createScriptURL(workerUrlWithNls) as unknown as string : workerUrlWithNls, { name: descriptor.label, type: 'module' });
	return whenESMWorkerReady(worker).finally(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(workerUrlWithNls));
```

I avoided the more common `new Worker(url); URL.revokeObjectURL(url);` idiom on purpose. That one depends on when the worker script fetch resolves the URL, and it has a history of cross-browser inconsistency. Using the ready hook that is already there needs no such assumption.

There is a second thing, independent of the leak. The bootstrap serialises the full NLS table into a 1.1 MB string on every worker creation. That content is deterministic for a given label and script URL, so caching one blob URL per bootstrap would make it bounded. Let me know if that is worth its own issue.

## Why this surfaces as disk usage

Blobs stay in memory until the renderer is under memory pressure, and Chromium then pages them into `blob_storage`. On a 16 GB machine with a lot of windows open they all end up on disk. The on-disk files pack four bootstraps each (I checked the offsets), so 3,203 files corresponded to roughly 12,800 retained blobs.

In #249343 the reporter was asked whether they had turned this setting on deliberately. In my case the answer is no: it came from `experiment: { mode: "startup" }`, and the first I knew about it was the 13 GB.

## Build failure

The unit test `LanguageModelAccess model info › publishes a core-only Luna alias for dictation cleanup without publishing hidden models directly` failed on `main`. It asserts `lunaPublishedDirectly: false` but observed `true`, so the hidden `gpt-5.6-luna` model was being published as a top-level, user-selectable language model.

## Root cause

The failure is a test-setup regression, not a production defect. In production, `AutomodeService.resolveAutoModePickerEndpoint` (`extensions/copilot/src/platform/endpoint/node/automodeService.ts`) always wraps the chosen base endpoint in an `AutoChatEndpoint`, which is published under the pseudo model id `auto`. A hidden model such as `gpt-5.6-luna` is therefore never surfaced directly in the model picker.

The test's `IAutomodeService` mock instead returned the raw `lunaEndpoint` from `resolveAutoModePickerEndpoint`. `LanguageModelAccess._provideLanguageModelChatInfo` then pushed that hidden endpoint into the published set under its own model id `gpt-5.6-luna`, making `lunaPublishedDirectly` true. The assertion was correct; the mock was infidelitous to production behavior.

## How the fix works

The mock now mirrors production by returning a real `AutoChatEndpoint` that wraps `lunaEndpoint`. The wrapper is instantiated from the test's instantiation service (all required services — `IDomainService`, `ICAPIClientService`, etc. — are provided by `createExtensionTestingServices`) after the testing accessor is created, and assigned to the closure variable the mock returns. A base-count cache entry for the `auto` pseudo model is pre-seeded (matching the existing pattern for the other endpoints) to keep the test deterministic and fast. With the wrapper in place, the picker endpoint publishes as `auto`, `gpt-5.6-luna` is no longer published directly, and the assertion passes.

## Rollback evaluation

Recommendation: **Do not roll back**.

Public culprit commit/PR: `83dfbdd3a9d94908ae3c92c3ec0ca34f2afe8dcf` (PR #331338). The originating change is a legitimate feature (a core-only Luna dictation-cleanup alias); only its accompanying test mock diverged from production behavior. A fix-forward on the test is bounded and safer than reverting the feature. Owners to consult: `@meganrogge`.

Automated validation (typecheck/test) could not be run in this environment because Node.js execution is blocked. The change was verified by source inspection against `automodeService.resolveAutoModePickerEndpoint`, `AutoChatEndpoint`, and `LanguageModelAccess._provideLanguageModelChatInfo`, confirming the mock now matches the production wrapping contract.

Low. The change is confined to a single test file's mock setup and does not touch production code.

<!-- 🪓 If you answered No above, use 'Help: Start Extension Bisect' from Command Palette to try to identify the cause. -->
<!-- 📣 Issues caused by an extension need to be reported directly to the extension publisher. The 'Help > Report Issue' dialog can assist with this. -->
- VS Code Version: 1.134.0
- OS Version: Windows 11

The `codeLoadingTime` reported to telemetry for extension activation time can be misleading--it is essentially a wall-clock time measurement around module load. For CJS extensions, this is a good approximation--since `require()` will be synchronous--but for ESM extensions, this breaks down. With ESM, if any other extensions are activating or working hard at the same time (which is highly likely especially at startup), then any work they are doing could be counted against your extension's code loading time, as their async work is interleaved with the async work of loading your extension code.

The bottom line is that ESM extension code loading time could be severely overstated in telemetry.

Having a truly accurate measurement would probably involve complex `async_hooks` / `AsyncLocalStorage` stuff, but a cheap approximation could be achieved just by including, e.g., some measures for event loop utilization/delay to estimate the contention, along with telemetry readers focusing on code loading measurements without much contention--so they can get a more "fair" understanding.

title: snap: stage libpulse0 so Chromium can use PulseAudio/PipeWire
body:
snap: stage `libpulse0` so Chromium can use PulseAudio/PipeWire

## Problem

Microphone capture does not work in the `code` snap on Linux. Speech-to-text
(`ms-vscode.vscode-speech`) fails with:

> Could not access the microphone for speech-to-text: Could not start audio source

The same failure affects anything that calls `getUserMedia()` in the snap.
Reproduced on Ubuntu 26.04 with VS Code 1.134.0 (snap rev 258), PipeWire 1.6.2
and `pipewire-pulse`. The microphone itself is fine — `pw-record` against the
default source captures audio normally, and Chrome (`.deb`) records without
issue on the same machine.

## Root cause

`resources/linux/snap/snapcraft.yaml` stages `libasound2` but not `libpulse0`,
and `core20` does not ship libpulse either:

```
$ ls /snap/core20/current/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/ | grep pulse
(nothing)
$ find /snap/code/258 -name 'libpulse*'
(nothing)
```

Chromium `dlopen()`s `libpulse.so.0` to select its PulseAudio backend. When that
fails it silently falls back to the ALSA backend. The snap's ALSA then has no
way to reach the sound server: the host routes the `default` device through
`libasound_module_pcm_pipewire.so`, and the snap runtime contains no
`alsa-lib/` plugin directory at all. Opening a capture device therefore fails,
surfacing as *"Could not start audio source"*.

The difference is visible by comparing the audio service of a working app with
the snap's:

```
# Chrome (.deb) — microphone works
$ grep -oE '/\S*lib(pulse|asound)\S*' /proc/$CHROME_AUDIO_PID/maps | sort -u
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libasound.so.2.0.0
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libpulse.so.0.24.3
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pulseaudio/libpulsecommon-17.0.so

# code snap — microphone fails
$ grep -oE '/\S*lib(pulse|asound)\S*' /proc/$CODE_AUDIO_PID/maps | sort -u
/snap/code/258/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libasound.so.2.0.0
```

No libpulse is mapped in the snap — only ALSA.

This is not distro-specific: it applies to any host where the microphone sits
behind PulseAudio or PipeWire, which is the default on current desktop Linux.
Users cannot work around it, because the host's libpulse targets a newer glibc
(2.43 on Ubuntu 26.04) than the `core20` runtime (2.31), so it cannot be
injected via `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.

## Fix

Add `libpulse0` to `stage-packages`. Snapcraft pulls in the transitive
dependencies that `core20` lacks (`libsndfile1`, `libasyncns0` and their
codec dependencies) and rewrites the `RUNPATH` of the staged libraries for
classic confinement, so `libpulsecommon` resolves inside the snap.

`libpulse0` is not present in `core20`, so the existing `cleanup` part will not
strip it from the prime directory.

## Verification

The `core20` build of libpulse is 13.99.1. To confirm that version can talk to a
current sound server, I extracted the focal `libpulse0` package — exactly what
snapcraft stages for `core20` — and opened a record stream against the host's
`pipewire-pulse` on Ubuntu 26.04:

```
loaded: libpulse-simple.so.0
PASS: connected to PulseAudio server, record stream open
PASS: read 6400 bytes of PCM, peak amplitude = 19

# libraries actually mapped:
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib/libpulse.so.0.21.2
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib/libpulsecommon-13.99.so
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib/libsndfile.so.1.0.28
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib/libasyncns.so.0.3.1
```

The PulseAudio wire protocol is stable, and `pipewire-pulse` serves the older
client without trouble.

I also confirmed the snap runtime can reach the socket, so the library is the
only missing piece:

```
$ echo 'echo $LD_LIBRARY_PATH; ls -d $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/pulse' | snap run --shell code
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib
/run/user/1000/pulse
```

## Risk

Low. One additional stage-package; the snap grows by roughly 1 MB. Behaviour is
unchanged on hosts without a PulseAudio server, where Chromium continues to fall
back to ALSA exactly as it does today.

I could not run a full snap build locally, so it is worth confirming on CI that
snapcraft's classic ELF patching resolves `libpulsecommon-13.99.so` from
`$SNAP/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pulseaudio/` in the built artefact.

title: Address review feedback on external session files removal
body:
Follow-ups to #332538, which removed external session files from the agent host adaptor. Each item addresses a review comment left on that PR.

### Release per-chat caches when a peer chat is removed

#332538 made per-chat parsing lazy, but the caches backing it — `outputByChat`, `lastTurnChangesByChat` and `customizationsByChat` — had no eviction path. When `_applyChatCatalog` drops a peer, the `AdditionalChat` is disposed, yet those maps retained that chat's observables and parser state for the lifetime of the adapter, so repeated chat creation/deletion leaked one object graph per deleted chat.

`ISessionOutputObs` gains a `releaseChat(chatUri)` method, called from the existing peer-pruning loop in `_applyChatCatalog`. That loop already iterates exactly the chats the catalog no longer lists and is reached before either return path, so it is the single place both removal routes pass through. Keys are protocol chat URIs, so the chat id is mapped back with `buildChatUri`.

### Correct stale API documentation

`IAgentFeedbackService.getSessionForFile` still documented the old behavior — that files outside the session's workspace folders return `undefined`. Since #332538 the only exclusion is output-channel resources, so the doc now says that rather than guiding consumers by obsolete behavior.

### Cover the lazy-subscription contract

The laziness introduced by #332538 was only exercised indirectly through the parser. Three regression tests now pin the actual contract using a recording `IAgentConnection` that tracks acquired and still-open subscription references:

- a chat that is never observed opens no subscription;
- observing one chat subscribes to that chat alone, and disposing the observer releases it;
- `releaseChat` drops the cached observables so a later request rebuilds them.

The first two would have failed under the pre-#332538 fan-out, and the third fails without the eviction fix above.

### Validation

`npm run typecheck-client` clean, and the `agentHostSessionFiles` suite passes with 11 tests including the 3 new ones.

title: agentHost: harden legacy Copilot CLI -> AH migration — freeze the gate, fix mid-migration handoff, clean up adopted sessions
body:
## What & why

Legacy Copilot CLI → Agent Host migration. Makes `chat.agentSessions.migrateLegacyCopilotCli` restart-frozen and fixes several
correctness/UX issues in how sessions hand off between the extension-host and Agent-Host providers. Normal and external sessions are unaffected.

## Changes

- **Setting frozen at startup.** The shared Agent Host survives window reload, so the   setting now applies only after a restart: renderer, extension host, and Agent Host each   read a one-time startup snapshot (via a new `BlockStartup` gate); the old live   enable/disable rediscovery machinery is removed. Setting is `APPLICATION`-scoped and the  relauncher prompts to restart on change.

- **No dropped rows mid-migration.** `AgentSessionsModel` preserves live-registered  (agent-host / remote) provider rows across a sibling's partial refresh. `AgentService`  surfaces an adopted row *before* the slower restore (never absent from both lists) and
  authoritatively refuses unregistered non-adoptable chats. The extension CLI provider  stands down only when the host would actually surface the row (a resumable target  exists), so a dead session is never orphaned; archived legacy sessions stay until opened.

- **Adopt-on-open UX.** The opener and `chatEditorInput` restore run the adopt probe under a  subtle "Opening chat…" progress hint, gated to migrated resources so normal opens stay  overhead-free; open/restore timeout budgets raised for a still-cold host.

- **Archived correctness.** Persisted archived state is rehydrated on item re-emit so an  archived row can't be resurrected; archived legacy sessions migrate on open.

- **Transcript cleanliness.** `mapSessionEvents` strips `<system-reminder>` scaffolding so  derived titles/previews aren't polluted.

title: agentHost: retry Codex model discovery after transient failures
body:
Fixes #331260

Codex can receive restored Copilot credentials while its first model-catalog request fails transiently. That leaves an existing session's model picker stale until another refresh trigger or a restart.

This change:
- retries Copilot-backed Codex model discovery with a bounded equal-jitter backoff
- invalidates scheduled retries when credentials, endpoints, or agent lifetime change
- preserves the last-known-good catalog during transient failures
- shares the retry policy with the Copilot agent
- adds regression coverage for a 503 followed by a successful refresh

## Testing
- `npm run transpile-client`
- focused Codex/Copilot model-refresh tests (30 passing)
- `npm run hygiene`
- manual sign-out/sign-in repro with a transient first catalog failure; the existing session picker populated after retry without restart

title: Remove external session files from the agent host adaptor
body:
The session adaptor derived an `externalFiles` observable — files the agent created, edited or deleted outside the workspace — and surfaced it as `ISession.externalChanges`. It was the only reader of `IChatFileEdits.allEdits`, and reading it forced a `StateComponents.Chat` subscription for **every peer chat** in the session plus a parse of **every completed turn**, purely to keep that list current.

This removes the feature and its three consumers, then simplifies the parsing it was holding up.

### Consumers removed

- **Chat pills** — `buildSessionArtifactSections` no longer takes an `externalFiles` argument, dropping the previewable-file/image merge loop.
- **Agent feedback** — `_isFileInSessionScope` becomes `_isFileEligibleForFeedback`: a file is eligible unless it is an output-channel resource. The `session.changes` lookup, the external-changes lookup and the workspace-folder containment check are gone.
- **Changes view** — the "Other Files" section is removed: `SessionFilesWidget`, `SessionFilesViewModel`, their CSS and fixture are deleted, and the `SplitView` drops from three panes to two (CI checks moves from index 2 to index 1).
- **Session model** — `ISession.externalChanges`, `ISessionFile` and `SessionFileOperation` are removed, along with both `visibleSessions.ts` wrapper getters.

### The perf win

With `allEdits` gone, two things in `agentHostSessionFiles.ts` fall away:

- **Per-chat subscriptions are now lazy.** The old `chatUrisObs` → `mapObservableArrayCached` fan-out read every chat's edits, and chat-state subscriptions are created on read — so an active session opened a subscription for every peer chat. Chats are now created on demand keyed by the requested chat URI, so a peer chat nobody reads costs nothing.
- **Only the last turn is parsed.** `createIncrementalChatFileEditsParser` no longer walks and memoizes every completed turn. It parses the active turn while streaming, or memoizes just the last completed turn by id. Turns that were never the last turn are never parsed at all.

Net **−1189 lines**.

### Notes

- **Agent feedback is a behaviour change, not just a deletion.** Feedback is now accepted on any open editor while a session is active, including files outside the workspace such as user settings. This is intended, but it is the case the old scoping existed to exclude.
- **The accessibility help was updated too.** `sessionsChangesAccessibilityHelp.ts` had two localized strings describing the Other Files section and its keyboard behaviour; leaving them would have had the screen-reader help dialog describe a section that no longer exists.
- **No collapse-state migration needed.** `otherFiles` is removed from `IChangesViewSectionCollapseState`; that state is in-memory only (`IStoredChangesViewState` persists just `detailsViewState`), so nothing stale is read back from storage.

### Validation

`npm run typecheck-client` clean; affected unit tests pass (118 + 194 + 16 across the sessions provider, changes view, chat artifacts, agent feedback and visible-sessions suites).

- VS Code Version: 1.134.0
- OS Version: Windows 11

# Description
This issue is regarding the newly introduced dictation function in VS Code. I have no specific steps on how to reproduce this unfortunately.

My company blocks automatic downloading of the Nemotron resulting in the following error message:
`Could not download the nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b speech-to-text model, which can happen on networks that block the model registry. You can install it from a downloaded package instead.`

The VS Code [website](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/configure/accessibility/voice#_install-the-model-from-a-local-package) mentions the following:
`If network restrictions prevent VS Code from downloading the on-device model, download the official CPU model package separately. Then run Chat: Install Dictation Model from Local Package... and select the ZIP file or prepared model folder.`

It is, however, not that trivial as to how to get this up and running manually. Maybe the documentation could be improved a bit in this regard. In any case, I'll describe how I got it to work eventually in case it is useful to others. I am not sure whether I have missed something completely that would simplify manual installation, but that would in any case then be useful to add to the documentation.

# Manual installation & issues
The first minor issue is that when browsing for the model, VS Code does not allow to select ".zip" files.

When searching for this model online, you'll only find the [Hugging Face repository](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b) of this model and the [NVIDIA webpage](https://build.nvidia.com/nvidia/nemotron-asr-streaming/modelcard), which refers to the same Hugging Face page. The problem is that the Hugging Face version of the model is not accepted by VS Code as it must be a specific ONNX version of the model. It was a bit difficult to find out how to obtain a suitable model. I now found a Microsoft [blogpost](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/foundry/foundry-local-v1-1/) on live transcriptions that provided some guidance.  The code I now use to download the model:
```python
"""
This script downloads a streaming speech model using Foundry Local.

Requirements:
    pip install foundry-local-sdk
"""

from pathlib import Path

from foundry_local_sdk import Configuration, FoundryLocalManager

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Initialize Foundry Local
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

cache_dir = Path(".") / "nemotron"
config = Configuration(
    app_name="fetch-vscode-dictation-model",
    model_cache_dir=str(cache_dir),
)
FoundryLocalManager.initialize(config)
manager = FoundryLocalManager.instance

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Download and load the streaming speech model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

model = manager.catalog.get_model("nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b")

if not model.is_cached:
    print("Downloading model...")
    model.download(lambda progress: print(f"\r  Progress: {progress:.1f}%", end="", flush=True))
    print("\n  Download complete.")

print(f"Model: {model.id}")
print(f"Prepared model folder: {model.get_path()}")
```

Selecting the cache directory of this model is accepted by VS Code and its files are saved to `%APPDATA%\Code\chatDictationModels\`. However, dictation still would not work as the same error message kept popping up. I found out that VS Code also needs a Foundry Local runtime that might be downloaded together with the model normally, which I cannot check myself. VS Code will, misleadingly, keep showing the error that the model must first be downloaded manually instead.

I now circumvented this by also downloading the runtime files manually here:
https://main.vscode-cdn.net/dictation-runtime/foundry-local/1.2.3/win32-x64.tgz
And extracting the files, such that:
```
%APPDATA%\Code\chatDictationRuntime\1.2.3\
├── .complete-win32-x64
├── prebuilds\win32-x64\foundry_local_napi.node
└── foundry-local-core\win32-x64\ (Foundry Local + onnxruntime DLLs)
```
Finally, the `.complete-win32-x64` file must be added manually to the directory above. It's contents must be set to `1.2.3`. After that, the dictation function started working for me.

title: files: stop Windows watcher flood after folder deletion
body:
## Summary

- detect the absolute watched-root path that Windows reports after a watched folder is deleted
- close the stale native watcher so repeated `rename` events cannot spin and flood process logs
- reattach directly when the folder was recreated before the delayed existence check completes
- cover permanent deletion, rapid delete/recreate, continued events after reattachment, and same-named children

## Motivation

Recent Agent Host sessions showed `agenthost.log` growing by roughly 2 MB every three seconds. The log was dominated by repeated events such as:

```
[File Watcher (node.js)] [raw] ["rename"] \\?\c:\Code\vscode.worktrees\...\.github\agents
```

Once the log reached its rotation threshold, this also produced 23,832 main-process errors in one session:

```
rotating_file_sink: failed renaming ...\agenthost.log to ...\agenthost.1.log: permission denied
```

On Windows, `fs.watch` reports the full extended watched path in a tight loop after folder deletion. The existing code compared the raw event only with the folder basename and continually postponed its deletion check, so it never recognized the watched root as deleted.

## Validation

- focused Node.js watcher regressions: 3 passing
- `npm run transpile-client`
- `npm run typecheck-client`
- reviewed through three passes with Claude Opus 5; all actionable findings addressed

title: Agents: Keep disconnected tunnels available for manual reconnect
body:
Fixes #332352

After explicitly disconnecting a tunnel, its ID is persisted in
`tunnelAgentHost.autoConnectSuppressedTunnels`.

This suppression is intended to prevent automatic reconnection, but it was also
used to filter the tunnel out when registering session providers. After a
reload, the online tunnel therefore disappeared from the host UI and `/agents`
displayed `No Host`, leaving no manual reconnection path.

This change keeps suppressed tunnels registered as providers while preserving
the existing suppression behavior:

- Disconnect still suppresses automatic reconnection.
- Startup does not automatically reconnect a suppressed tunnel.
- The tunnel remains visible as disconnected and can be selected manually.
- An explicit reconnect clears the suppression.

A regression test covers disconnecting, restoring the tunnel cache after a
reload, skipping automatic reconnection, keeping the provider visible, and
clearing suppression on explicit reconnect.

title: Power-save blocker does not cover custom LanguageModelChatProvider models
body:
The power-save blocker added for #276546 does not appear to cover Agent sessions that use models provided by third-party `LanguageModelChatProvider` extensions.

The implementation in commit `de441dc178462184fb8772bfff47d325f752bf3e` acquires the power-save blocker in `ChatMLFetcher`, i.e. around model requests made through Copilot's own fetch path.

However, when an Agent session uses a model registered by another extension through `LanguageModelChatProvider`, the model request is handled by that provider instead and does not pass through `ChatMLFetcher`.

As a result, the computer can still go to sleep while such an Agent session is actively working.

### Example

I am using a Codex model exposed to Copilot Chat through the third-party Universal Chat Provider extension.

The effective path is roughly:

```text
Copilot Agent
    ↓
VS Code LanguageModelChatProvider API
    ↓
third-party model provider
    ↓
Codex
```

An Agent task can be actively running through this provider, but Windows still goes to sleep according to the configured idle timeout.

### Expected behavior

The power-save blocker should ideally follow the **Agent execution lifecycle**, independent of which language-model provider is being used.

While at least one Agent session is actively working, VS Code should prevent automatic system sleep.

This should include activity such as:

```text
model request
→ tool call
→ terminal command
→ file operation
→ model request
→ tests/build
→ model request
```

The display should still be allowed to turn off normally.

Sleep inhibition should be released once the Agent session has:

* finished;
* been cancelled; or
* reached a state where it is waiting for user interaction.

### Why the Agent/session layer may be preferable

The current implementation is tied to individual model requests and keeps the blocker alive for a grace period after a request completes.

That works for many cases, but it has two limitations:

1. **Third-party model providers are not covered** if their requests bypass `ChatMLFetcher`.
2. **Long-running tool calls may outlive the grace period**, even though the Agent itself is still actively working.

For example:

```text
model response finishes
→ build/test command runs for several minutes
→ next model request
```

The Agent is active for the entire period, but a blocker attached only to model fetching cannot reliably represent that state.

Moving or additionally applying the power-save blocker at the Agent/session execution level would make the behavior provider-independent and would cover the complete Agent workflow.

### Multiple VS Code windows

This should also work when multiple VS Code windows are open.

If any window has an Agent session that is actively working, the system should remain awake. Normal sleep should resume only after there are no actively working Agent sessions in any window.

### Related

* #276546
* Commit: `de441dc178462184fb8772bfff47d325f752bf3e`

This is not intended to duplicate #276546, but to report a gap in its current implementation for custom language-model providers and for Agent activity occurring between model requests.

title: Cache active-session external changes in AgentFeedbackService scope checks
body:
## Description

Loading or reopening a large Agent Host session generated thousands of duplicate child-chat subscriptions (~343 MB of AHP traffic, ~1,005 retained chat-state snapshots vs. a 42 MB / 78 snapshot baseline).

`AgentFeedbackService._isFileInSessionScope` runs for every visible editor and read `session.externalChanges?.get()`. That observable is subscription-backed (`createSessionOutputObs` → `externalFiles` → `editsPerChatObs` → `createActiveSessionSubscriptionObs`, which registers the AHP subscription ref on `reader.store`). A derived with zero observers computes *without caching* and then disposes its reader store, so every scope check acquired and immediately released one chat-state subscription **per chat** in the session — 39 chats × every visible changed-file editor.

```ts
// before: one uncached recomputation of the whole chain per scope check
if (session.externalChanges?.get().some(file => isEqual(file.uri, resourceUri))) {
	return true;
}
```

### Changes

- **Read from a kept-observed derived** — `_activeSessionExternalFiles` derives the active session's external files once and is held observed via `keepObserved`, so repeated scope checks hit the cache instead of re-subscribing. It stays lazy: nothing subscribes until the first out-of-workspace file is actually checked.
- **Reset on session switch** — the observation is re-established on active-session change (keyed on the session resource) and released on dispose, so the previous session's subscriptions drop immediately rather than being pinned. Note the ordering: `MutableDisposable.value = keepObserved(...)` evaluates the new observation *before* disposing the old one, which would never let the observer count reach zero, so the handle is `clear()`ed first.
- **External check runs last** — reordered `_isFileInSessionScope` so the changes/workspace-folder branches short-circuit first. Behaviour is unchanged (every preceding branch already returned `true`), but files inside the session workspace now never touch the external-changes chain at all.
- **Gated on the active session** — `externalFiles` is already gated on `isActiveSession && !isArchived` in the agent host provider, and other providers leave `externalChanges` undefined, so a non-active session returns `[]` either way.

### Test

`computes the session external changes once for repeated scope checks` counts recomputations and reader-store disposals through a derived that mirrors the provider's per-chat subscription. Three scope checks yield 1 computation / 0 releases; switching the active session releases them. Against the pre-fix read the same test reports 3 computations / 3 acquire-release cycles.

Fixes #332507

Every `*` in a fuzzy quick pick query became its own unbounded `.*` in the converted regexp. A run of adjacent stars made matching super-polynomial - the engine explores every composition of the haystack across the wildcards before failing near the end:

- `matchesFuzzy('********b', 'a'.repeat(28))`: about 1.4 s

This freezes the renderer while typing in any picker routed through `matchesFuzzy`. Runs of adjacent stars now collapse to a single wildcard (`/\*+/g -> '.*'`), which is language-preserving: `.*.*` accepts exactly what `.*` does, so no observable match span changes. A 300,000 case randomized old-vs-new comparison of match spans found zero differences.

Known open follow-up (not addressed here): queries with many *separated* wildcards (`a*b*c*d*e*f*g*h`) can still backtrack exponentially on adversarial labels. Unlike the `fuzzyScore` path, which caps input at `_maxLen = 128`, the regexp path has no cap; that deserves its own discussion since capping changes semantics for long legitimate queries.

Draft until #332507 receives triage.

```
exit 0

```

- New filters tests pin that `'**b'`, `'***'` behave exactly like `'*b'`, `'*'`.

title: Quick pick filter freezes on queries with runs of * wildcards
body:
### Bug description

`matchesFuzzy` (src/vs/base/common/filters.ts) supports `*` wildcards in quick pick queries by converting the query with `strings.convertSimple2RegExpPattern`, which replaces every `*` with its own `.*`. A query containing a run of adjacent stars therefore produces N adjacent unbounded quantifiers, and matching becomes super-polynomial: the regexp engine explores every composition of the haystack across the wildcards before failing near the end.

Measured on this machine against the real compiled module:

- `matchesFuzzy('********b', 'a'.repeat(28))`: about 1.4 seconds
- 12 stars against 40 characters: over two minutes
- simulated 20,000 label picker with query `*****com`: about 2.5 seconds per keystroke

This freezes the renderer while typing in any quick access that routes through `matchesFuzzy` (views, commands-adjacent pickers, debug pickers, icon labels).

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open a quick input that filters with fuzzy matching.
2. Type several `*` characters in a row followed by a letter that does not match, e.g. `********z`.
3. Observe input latency grow combinatorially with each additional star.

### Expected behavior

Adjacent wildcards should behave like a single wildcard. Collapsing runs of `*` to one `*` leaves the matched language identical (`.*.*` accepts exactly what `.*` does) and removes this class of hang entirely; measured to under a millisecond for the cases above after the change.

### Version tested

Commit `77f86f3d3a0` on `main`. Note a second, related backtracking surface remains open afterwards: many *separated* wildcards (`a*b*c*d*e*f*g*h`) can still backtrack exponentially on adversarial labels. The regex path has no length cap today, unlike the `fuzzyScore` path which caps at `_maxLen = 128`; that deserves its own discussion.

title: Context key scanner rejects the d and v regex flags in when clauses
body:
### Bug description

The context key expression scanner whitelists which regex flags may follow a regex literal in a `when` clause (`src/vs/platform/contextkey/common/scanner.ts`, `_regexFlags`). The set is

```ts
['i', 'g', 's', 'm', 'y', 'u']
```

which is missing the two newer ECMAScript flags: `d` (hasIndices) and `v` (unicodeSets). Both are valid in the engines VS Code ships on, but a when clause that uses them fails to lex: the trailing flag character is not consumed as part of the regex token, becomes a separate `Str` token, the parser then reports "Expected: REGEX", and `ContextKeyExpr.deserialize` returns `undefined` for a perfectly legal clause.

Example: an extension manifest containing

```json
"when": "a =~ /x/d"
```

silently evaluates to never-match today.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Add a keybinding or view with `"when": "editorTextFocus =~ /x/d"` (any regex using the `d` or `v` flag).
2. Observe the clause never activates; enabling context key tracing shows it deserialized to undefined.

Flags from the whitelist (`/x/i`, `/x/gm`) work as expected.

### Expected behavior

All ECMAScript regex flags accepted by the runtime should lex, parse and deserialize, so `/x/d` and `/x/v` clauses behave like `/x/i`.

### Version tested

Commit `77f86f3d3a0` on `main`. Reproduced at the unit level: scanning `'foo =~ /zee/d'` yields a trailing `Str 'd'` token instead of a single `RegexStr '/zee/d'`. A fix plus scanner tests and an end-to-end deserialize test is ready.

title: Git: getRemoteRefs returns remote head refs with name and commit swapped
body:
### Bug description

`Git.getRemoteRefs()` (extensions/git/src/git.ts) parses `git ls-remote` output and builds `Ref` objects. For remote **heads** the mapping is inverted:

```ts
if (match = /^([0-9a-f]{40})\trefs\/heads\/([^ ]+)$/.exec(line)) {
    return { name: match[1], commit: match[2], type: RefType.Head };
}
```

Group 1 of that regex is the 40 character SHA and group 2 is the branch name, so every returned head has the SHA in `name` and the branch name in `commit`. The tags branch three lines below does it the right way round (`name: match[2], commit: match[1]`), which confirms the intent.

Example: for the line

```
52c293a05038d865604c2284aa8698bd087915a1	refs/heads/main
```

the function returns `{ name: '52c293a05038d865604c2284aa8698bd087915a1', commit: 'refs/heads/main' }` where it should return `{ name: 'main', commit: '52c293a05038d865604c2284aa8698bd087915a1' }`.

The only in-repo caller currently passes `{ tags: true }`, so the broken heads path is dormant today, but the method is part of the extension's repository surface and any use of `getRemoteRefs(remote, { heads: true })` gets unusable data.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Call `repository.getRemoteRefs('<remote>', { heads: true })` against any remote with at least one branch.
2. Inspect the returned array: `name` holds SHAs, `commit` holds ref names like `refs/heads/main`.

### Expected behavior

Head entries follow the documented `Ref` shape: `name` is the branch name, `commit` is the SHA, matching what the same function already produces for tags.

### Version tested

Commit `77f86f3d3a0` on `main`. Found by reading the parser and pinned with a unit test (`parseLsRemote`) that exercises real `ls-remote` output format; a fix is ready including regression tests for heads, tags, mixed input and multiple heads.

title: Agent Host session load causes child-chat subscription storm and memory spike

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Issue identified by VS Code Team member as probable bug

labels.name: verified

labels.description: VS Code crashing, performance, freeze and memory leak issues

body:
## Summary

Loading and reopening a large Agent Host session can generate thousands of duplicate child-chat subscriptions, causing a sharp renderer/transport memory spike and hundreds of MB of AHP traffic.

## Reproduction

Using the session **Agent Host session migration** (39 subagent chats):

1. Open the session and wait for history/Changes to settle.
2. Open another session.
3. Reopen the original session.

Controlled runs with isolated copies of the same profile:

| Build | AHP bytes | Child-chat snapshots |
|---|---:|---:|
| `43c9cf468f20` (good Insiders) | 42.3 MB | 78 |
| `fc62850c022b` (bad Insiders) | 343.2+ MB | 1,005 retained after rotation |

## Bisect and root cause

A source-level bisect identified commit `38220eab177286ceaf47098a843396d351464247` (#331079):

| Source revision | AHP bytes | Child-chat snapshots |
|---|---:|---:|
| Parent `30ad9a507bd` | 42.9 MB | 85 |
| `38220eab177` | 367.7 MB | 864 |

The triggering change is the new synchronous external-changes scope check in `AgentFeedbackService._isFileInSessionScope`:

```ts
if (session.externalChanges?.get().some(file => isEqual(file.uri, resourceUri))) {
    return true;
}
```

`externalChanges` is subscription-backed. Calling `.get()` while it is unobserved recomputes its dependencies for each visible changed-file editor, transiently acquiring and releasing all child-chat subscriptions. The target session has 39 child chats, so repeated file scope checks create a large overlapping subscribe/unsubscribe storm.

Line-level verification on `38220eab177`:

- Removing only the new `externalChanges.get()` check: **43.0 MB / 87 child snapshots** (baseline restored).
- Removing the separate new subagent annotation-restore await instead: **375.1 MB / 866 child snapshots** (still reproduces).

Confidence in this causal attribution is very high; the immediate-parent, child, and single-expression A/B tests were all run against the same profile and automated scenario.

title: macOS 15: Space in the save-changes dialog hits Cancel instead of Don't Save
body:
On macOS 15, Space in the "Do you want to save the changes you made to X?" dialog now activates **Cancel** instead of **Don't Save**.

The muscle memory this breaks is Enter = save, Space = discard, Esc = go back — three one-key answers to a three-way question, none of which needs the mouse. Space is the one that silently changed meaning: the same keystroke that used to discard the file now dismisses the dialog and leaves the editor open. It fails quietly, so you find out by pressing it twice and wondering why the tab is still there.

### Cause

`massageMessageBoxOptions` used to move the cancel button to index 1 on every macOS. NSAlert lays out `[0]` on the right, `[1]` on the left and the rest in between, so the buttons rendered horizontally with the focus ring on "Don't Save":

```
[ Cancel ][ Don't Save ][ Save ]
   Esc       Space        Enter
```

https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/commit/a064657382897f532319984f13ffbb68743a45fe ("Remove legacy reordering for native dialogs on macOS", #327337) gates that reordering behind Darwin < 24, so macOS 15+ now gets the array unchanged: `[Save, Don't Save, Cancel]`. Three equal buttons make NSAlert stack them vertically, and the focus ring lands on the last one — Cancel.

Enter and Esc survive because Electron assigns those key equivalents explicitly (`setKeyEquivalent:@"\r"` on `default_id`, `@"\e"` on `cancel_id` in `shell/browser/ui/message_box_mac.mm`). "Don't Save" has never had a key equivalent — it only ever inherited the ring from its position, which is why removing the reordering removed the shortcut with it.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. On macOS 15 or later, edit a file so the tab is dirty.
2. `Cmd+W`.
3. Press Space.

Expected: changes discarded, tab closes (behaviour before the linked commit).
Actual: dialog is cancelled, tab stays open with the changes.

### Notes

The vertical button stack is itself a symptom: a native macOS save alert is horizontal, with Cancel on the left and the destructive alternative in the middle. Reverting to that layout restores the ring for free. Giving "Don't Save" an explicit key equivalent would be an independent fix, and arguably the more durable one, since it would not depend on AppKit's key-view loop at all.

Verified locally by raising the Darwin bound in `out/main.js`: the horizontal layout and Space returned.

---

- macOS 15.1 (Darwin 24.1.0)

title: chat: summarize the Agent Merge prompt as a widget
body:
Agent Merge drives its repair turns with a machine-facing `<agent_merge_state>` block, which the transcript rendered verbatim — a wall of protocol text where the user expected a status update.

This extracts the prompt builder into `agentMergePrompt.ts` next to a matching parser, and renders the recovered state as a collapsible card.

### Collapsed
A single line naming the work and why it is happening.

### Expanded
The pull request, the review feedback, the failing checks, and a nested `Agent message` disclosure holding the verbatim instructions sent to the agent.

## Details

- **Parser lives with the builder.** `buildAgentMergePrompt` moved out of `agentMergeController.ts` so the format has one owner. The parser reads the state block **backwards from its end**, so untrusted feedback bodies (emitted before the trailing fields) cannot shift a later field boundary; a thread whose body mimics the prompt format stays one comment.
- **Untrusted markdown.** Review feedback renders through `ChatContentMarkdownRenderer`, so inline code, lists and links work while trusted command links stay off.
- **File labels.** Comments are labelled by file name, gaining the shortest distinguishing directory prefix only when several comments share a name — the same `shorten()` disambiguation editor tabs use.
- **Linked comments.** Prompt thread ids are exactly the `sourcePRReviewCommentId` the PR-review seeder stores, so matched labels reveal the local comment in the editor via one new command on the existing chat↔sessions bridge. Guarded on `CommandsRegistry`, so the regular workbench renders unchanged.
- **Checks link to GitHub.** Each failing check opens the pull request's checks tab. A per-run deep link would require adding `detailsUrl` to the model-facing prompt, so the prompt was left untouched.

## Testing

- 5 parser tests, including a build/parse round trip and an untrusted-feedback spoofing case.
- 3 tests for the file-label disambiguation.
- 12 component fixtures (Dark + Light) covering collapsed, expanded, comments-only, checks-only, conflicting, behind-base, markdown, duplicate file names, linked comments, and the expanded agent message.

title: sessions: share the session hover between the sessions list and chat pills
body:
The sessions list hover was an ad-hoc markdown string. It showed the source repository rather than the worktree a session actually works in, never used the word "Worktree", listed no pull requests, and named only the provider. It also could not be reused anywhere else.

## What changed

A shared `SessionSummaryHoverWidget` in the workbench layer renders provider-neutral `ISessionSummaryHoverData`, plus a small per-window `ISessionSummaryHoverService` registry so `agent-host-session://` pills in chat output show the same hover. Each window adapts its own data source onto that shape and omits what it cannot answer:

- Agents window: `ISession` -> hover data (`sessionHoverContent.ts`), the richest source.
- Editor window: `IChatSessionItem` -> hover data, which carries no worktree or pull requests, so those rows are simply absent.

## New layout

```
Fix authentication redirect loop          <- title only, no icon
 folder    \home\user\projects\vscode
 worktree  Worktree - \home\...\vscode.worktrees\fix-auth-redirect
 branch    fix-auth-redirect - 2 files changed +132 -18
------------------------------------------
 PR icon   Fix authentication redirect loop        <- live state colors
 PR icon   Add a regression test for the redirect loop
 PR icon   Revert the earlier redirect workaround
------------------------------------------
Claude - Local Agent Host                 <- dimmed
```

Separators only appear between blocks that exist, so a session with no pull requests gets one rule and a quick chat none. Despite carrying more information, it stays about as compact as before.

## Supporting model change

`IGitHubPullRequestRef` gained `title` and `createdByThisSession`. The agent-host provider populates both: titles come from the PR artifact labels the agent recorded, and `createdByThisSession` is the "main eligible" set (PRs the agent created plus PRs found for the session branch), excluding ones inherited from the checkout or merely referenced. Only pull requests the session produced are listed. Secondary PRs now also pick up their last-known state icon from `IPullRequestIconCache`, since only the main PR is polled live.

## Validation

- `tsc --noEmit` clean, eslint clean, stylelint clean, `valid-layers-check` passes
- 227 passing in the affected suites (`OpenSessionLinkOpenerContribution`, `LocalAgentHostSessionsProvider`, `SessionsLifecycleTracker`), including a new test that the pill hover data resolves through the registered provider
- New component fixtures (`sessions/sessionHover`) cover both data sources plus the empty cases, verified visually in the component explorer

title: Feature Request: Expose settings.json configuration for integrated browser proxy

labels.name: feature-request
labels.description: Request for new features or functionality

labels.name: browser-integration
labels.description: Web browsing features integrated into VS Code (e.g. integrated browser)

body:
<!-- ⚠️⚠️ Do Not Delete This! feature_request_template ⚠️⚠️ -->
<!-- Please read our Rules of Conduct: https://opensource.microsoft.com/codeofconduct/ -->
<!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates. -->

<!-- Describe the feature you'd like. -->


### Problem
VS Code integrated browser does not respect VS Code proxy settings.

The `http.proxy` / `http.noProxy` in settings.json only applies to VS Code itself, extensions and marketplace traffic. They have zero effect for the built‑in integrated browser.
Currently the integrated browser can only use OS‑level system proxy, with no dedicated proxy configuration inside VS Code.

This creates painful workflow gaps for frontend developers.

#### Real‑world critical use‑case 1: Local development with Whistle
Many frontend developers rely on whistle, a local HTTP debugging proxy, for daily work:
‑ Intercept requests
‑ Mock or rewrite API responses
‑ Map production hostnames to local backend services
‑ Modify request headers and capture HTTPS traffic.

When previewing application inside VS Code integrated browser, none of these whistle rules take effect. There is no way to configure the browser to use whistle from within VS Code settings.

Turning on global system‑wide proxy is not acceptable: it routes all other system applications through the proxy and disrupts normal daily usage.

#### Real‑world critical use‑case 2: AI‑assisted web debugging
We cannot simply open the page in an external browser.

The integrated browser is required for VS Code Agent / Copilot AI web debugging workflows:
‑ Only the built‑in browser can share live DOM, console logs, screenshots and page context directly into Copilot chat and agent sessions.
‑ External browsers cannot feed live page context to VS Code AI agents.

If integrated browser cannot use whistle proxy, AI agents observe raw unmocked backend responses instead of our actual local debugging environment. Developers have to manually copy and paste logs back‑and‑forth, which completely breaks the end‑to‑end AI‑driven debugging workflow.

### Proposed solution
Add dedicated user/workspace settings for integrated browser proxy inside settings.json, for example:
‑ `workbench.browser.proxy`
‑ `workbench.browser.proxyBypassList`

These settings should control the proxy used by the integrated browser. It is acceptable if changing these settings requires restarting VS Code to take effect due to underlying Chromium/Electron technical constraints.

### Alternatives considered
‑ System‑wide OS proxy: pollutes network for all other applications, not viable for day‑to‑day development.
‑ Open page in external browser: loses AI agent context‑sharing capability, defeats the purpose of using the integrated browser.

### Additional context
Local window scenario, not remote SSH/WSL.
Typical whistle proxy address: `http://127.0.0.1:8899`.

title: Copilot start a new session and consume tokens automatically
body:
- Copilot Chat Extension Version: built in
- VS Code Version: 1.134.0
- OS Version:Ubuntu 24.04
- Feature (agent mode):
- Selected model (any):
- Logs: None

Steps to Reproduce:

1. Choose Plan to generate any plan.
2. Choose 'Autocopilot' to run the Plan. Wait to finish.
3. Click the `<-` to back to the session list, or click the "+" to create a new session.
4. with about 70%~80% chance, the Copilot start a new session and add "Start implementation" as a normal chat message and start to run the agent automatically.

It's a huge waste of tokens! Hope someone fix this quickly.
I found this from 1.130.0 , and maybe it exists earlier.
